introduction: The guide turns on a sentence of Bahá’u’lláh: “They slay Husayn and then weep for him.” Its readings honour the grandson of Muḥammad who was killed at Karbila in 680, tell his thirst, the captivity of his family and the refusal of burial, and then ask what remembrance is worth when the mourners repeat the deed. Most of the company here has stood at a similar place. The Gospels and the psalms supply the cup, the thirst, the friends who slept and the judge’s unanswered question; Jesus tells the women to weep for themselves and charges the builders of prophets’ tombs. Antigone speaks for the unburied, Priam kisses the hand that killed his son, Lowell sets truth on the scaffold, and Gibbon admits that the scene will move the coldest reader. Against the readings stand Nietzsche, for whom blood proves nothing, Wilfred Owen’s “old Lie,” the Preacher’s one event for the righteous and the wicked, and Hopkins’s question about what any mourner mourns.
questions: Bahá’u’lláh says “They slay Husayn and then weep for him,” and Jesus says of the builders of prophets’ tombs that they witness against themselves. How can a community tell whether its remembrance is changing its conduct?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls a man torn to pieces victorious, and Lowell says the scaffold sways the future. Jeremiah still asks why the wicked prosper. What kind of victory do the readings claim, and what would count as evidence for it?
The sacrifice at Karbila is called “a complete proof,” while Nietzsche calls blood the worst witness of truth. What can a martyrdom show, and what can it not?
“Pass beyond fear and hope … enter the Karbila of love manfully.” Set this beside Rábi‘a’s prayer and Wilfred Owen’s warning. What distinguishes love that accepts death from the glorifying of death?
The dead of Karbila were left unburied; Antigone defies a king to bury her brother, and Achilles gives Hector’s body back to Priam. What do these stories say about what is owed even to an enemy?

Joseph’s story ends with “ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good,” and Proverbs forbids rejoicing when an enemy falls. How might those two sayings shape the way a wronged community tells its history?

outside.why: He gave life, kindred and possessions “that He might teach the friends of God the way of divine love.” Jesus names the same measure of love on the night before his own death: that a man lay down his life for his friends.
“By what measure shall I weep for thee?” Jeremiah wishes his head were waters and his eyes a fountain of tears, that he might weep day and night for the slain of his people.
The Báb says that all the seas of creation would not equal the weeping owed. Lamentations lets the stricken city speak for herself: behold, and see if there be any sorrow like unto my sorrow.
They lament every year and curse the oppressors, and oppress in their turn. Jesus says it of those who garnish the tombs of the prophets and are sure they would never have shed their blood.
“They slay Husayn and then weep for him.” Jesus, on the way to his death, turns to the women who bewail him: weep not for me, but weep for yourselves, and for your children.
“What advantage did the wicked Yazid derive from his vast empire?” The question in the Gospel has the same form: what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?

The reading is sure who gained and who lost. Jeremiah, who believes in the same justice, still has to ask it to its face: wherefore doth the way of the wicked prosper? How long may a believer go on asking?

“The abasement and lowliness of the Prince of Martyrs … was the glory of both worlds.” Paul’s hymn has the same turn: he humbled himself and became obedient unto death, wherefore God also hath highly exalted him.
Lowliness in the desert as sovereignty. Paul generalizes it for Corinth: God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty.
The poisoned arrow at the beginning, everlasting glory at the end. Paul weighs affliction against “a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory,” looking at the things which are not seen.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls a man whose body was torn to pieces victorious and quotes this verse. Here it is in its place in the Qur’án, where the help promised follows messengers who were first denied.
“No one can wrong him or usurp his right.” Socrates, condemned, tells his judges something close: no evil can happen to a good man, either in life or after death.
“Were it not for Thee, the fragrance of divine knowledge would have been cut off.” Hebrews says of its own tortured and slain witnesses: of whom the world was not worthy.

To visit Husayn’s shrine knowing his station is “like one who has visited God.” The women who came to another tomb were asked: why seek ye the living among the dead? What does a grave give that the angels’ question seems to refuse?
Prostration “upon the soil of Husayn.” The oldest scriptural warrant for honouring a piece of ground is the voice from the bush: the place whereon thou standest is holy ground.
On hearing the visitation the friends become “the companions of tearful eyes.” Paul makes it a rule of fellowship: rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.
Tears “like the clouds of springtime” for one slain long ago. Zechariah foresees a mourning of this kind: they shall look upon him whom they have pierced, and mourn as for an only son.
The commemoration is kept, and “other practices” of the season are called a grievous error. Joel had drawn the same line for mourners: rend your heart, and not your garments.
“The true account of Husayn … as ye hear tell each day and hour.” Gibbon, no friend to religious enthusiasm, told it in 1788 and added that it will awaken the sympathy of the coldest reader.

“Surrounded by enemies on the plain.” When Elisha’s servant sees a city compassed with horses, the prophet answers that they that be with us are more, and the young man’s eyes are opened. At Karbila no such army intervenes. What then does “with us” mean?
A thirst that all creation could not comprehend. The psalmist looked for some to take pity, and found none: in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.

The victors “were happy and joyful … constantly boasting before friend and stranger.” David’s lament for Saul and Jonathan dreads exactly this: tell it not in Gath, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice.

The family of the Prophet led captive to Damascus. The exiles of Judah remembered such a road: by the rivers of Babylon we sat down and wept, and they that carried us away captive required of us a song.

Exile, plunder, captivity and death are called a table on which “every kind of food was present.” Jesus uses the sister image when he is arrested: the cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it?
They were left “covered in blood and mixed with dust.” A psalm mourns the same outrage in Jerusalem: their blood have they shed like water, and there was none to bury them.
The dead of Karbila were refused burial. Antigone, who buried her brother against the king’s order, appeals to laws that no ruler made: the unwritten and unfailing statutes of heaven.
In the Iliad the enemy’s body is given back: old Priam kisses the hands that killed his son, and Achilles weeps with him. What had to be present in that tent that was absent on the plain?

“Injury and trials and pillage and affliction and supreme martyrdom.” A psalm, quoted again by Paul, says it in one line: for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter.
Companions and their descendants arose to kill him, persuaded that he had broken God’s law. Jesus warns his disciples of that sincerity: whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service.
“It was all due to prejudiced tales and stories.” The charge prepared against Stephen is of the same make: we have heard him speak blasphemous words against this holy place and the law.
“For what crime did you martyr the son …?” Micah hears God put the same question to a people: O my people, what have I done unto thee? Testify against me.
“Did my Hasan deal faithlessly amongst you?” Jesus, with the stones already in their hands: many good works have I shewed you; for which of those works do ye stone me?
“For what crime did ye slay my Husayn?” In Matthew it is the judge who asks, and gets no answer but the cry repeated: why, what evil hath he done?
“The Concourse on High lamented.” The psalm says how such a death is counted above: precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.

A blessing on the one who visits the grave and remembers. Pericles, burying the Athenian dead, says that the whole earth is the tomb of famous men, whose record is unwritten in other men’s hearts. Which remembrance does a grave serve?

What befell the Prophet’s descendants at Karbila has now befallen another household. The First Letter of Peter tells its readers not to think the fiery trial strange, but to see whose sufferings they share.
A woman is told that she is the return of Husayn’s wife in what she has borne. Simeon tells the mother of Jesus her part beforehand: a sword shall pierce through thy own soul also.
Husayn is seen in Abel, slain “with the sword of hatred” by his brother. Genesis gives the first such death its own voice: the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground.
“Yet do We yield Him thanks for all that He hath destined.” Job, with nothing left, says the hardest form of it: though he slay me, yet will I trust in him.
The Báb reads Joseph as Husayn. Here is the moment in Genesis the reading turns on: the brothers see him afar off and say, Behold, this dreamer cometh; come now therefore, and let us slay him.
Joseph in the Qur’án, the chapter on which the Báb is commenting: the brothers bring a shirt with false blood on it, and Jacob answers with “comely patience.”
Joseph as one sent ahead through suffering. A psalm reads his story that way: he sent a man before them, who was sold for a servant, whose feet they hurt with fetters.
“Did not the Truth come to you … after he had proclaimed unto you … God’s most great Cause?” In Jesus’s parable the husbandmen know exactly who has come: this is the heir; come, let us kill him.
“Did he not humbly seek water for himself and for his infant child?” The charge at the judgment in Matthew is the same refusal: I was thirsty, and ye gave me no drink.

The story of Joseph ends in a way the reading does not reach: he forgives his brothers, saying, ye thought evil against me, but God meant it unto good. Can the story of Karbila be read to that end, and by whom?
“This is Husayn Who hath appeared among you … yet ye recognized not His worth.” John’s prologue has the sentence for every such coming: he came unto his own, and his own received him not.
Bahá’u’lláh claims the return of Husayn and says it went unrecognized. Jesus says of the return of Elijah: Elias is come already, and they knew him not, but have done unto him whatsoever they listed.
They count a martyrdom long past as proof and are “heedless … of that which has come to pass in these days.” Jesus: ye can discern the face of the sky, but can ye not discern the signs of the times?

Seventy-two died at Karbila, “while here thousands stepped into the field of martyrdom.” Tertullian made the argument to Rome’s governors about 197: the oftener we are mown down, the more we grow; the blood of Christians is seed.

The sacrifice is called “a complete proof.” Nietzsche denies that dying for a cause proves anything about it: blood is the worst of all witnesses to the truth. What exactly does a martyrdom prove, and what does it not?

“The water of life was flowing … but there was not a thirsty soul to be found.” Jesus cries the invitation in the temple on the last day of the feast: if any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink.

The reading describes water without thirst. Amos foretells the reverse: a famine of hearing the words of the Lord, when they shall run to and fro to seek it and shall not find it. Which of the two is our own case?
“Is there anyone … who will come to aid me?” In Gethsemane Jesus finds his friends asleep: what, could ye not watch with me one hour?
The cry on the field of Karbila went unanswered. Isaiah gives the words to a lone figure: I looked, and there was none to help; and I wondered that there was none to uphold.
The Báb sees the severed head of the Imam hanging on a tree. Mark tells how the head of John the Baptist was brought on a dish to a king’s feast, and how his disciples came for the body.
The Imam’s son, wandering the desert with bare head and bare feet, is set up as an example. Jesus says of himself: the foxes have holes, but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.

Abasement became eternal glory, and the tyrant’s glory abasement. Lowell’s lines, written against slavery in 1845: Truth forever on the scaffold, Wrong forever on the throne, yet that scaffold sways the future.

“Hast thou ever heard mention of his other days?” Only the day of suffering is remembered. George Eliot ends Middlemarch by honouring the opposite kind of life: unhistoric acts, a hidden life, and unvisited tombs. Which does the world owe more to?
Kings are killed and forgotten; one killed in the path of God is lamented for thirteen hundred years. Proverbs: the memory of the just is blessed, but the name of the wicked shall rot.

“How many kings are killed but there is no mention of them.” Shakespeare’s Richard II sits on the ground to tell sad stories of the death of kings, and is himself remembered for it. Why do some deaths of the powerful move us after all?
“All their palaces and royal residences are ruined and not one trace is left.” Khayyám, in FitzGerald’s verse, finds the lion and the lizard keeping the courts where Jamshyd gloried.
“Yazid too departed this world, and the Lord of the Martyrs likewise … what a difference between them!” Jesus’s parable follows a rich man and a beggar past the same door and shows the difference.

The reading sees a great difference between two deaths. The Preacher, looking only at what is under the sun, sees none: there is one event to the righteous, and to the wicked. What does each of them refuse to look at?

The site was razed and ploughed for eighty years and still came back. Gamaliel’s advice to the council in Jerusalem states the test: if this work be of men, it will come to nought; but if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it.
“His martyrdom became a support and champion” to the Law of the Messenger. Jesus’s figure for a death that bears: except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone.
Unbearable trials were “most sweet” in his palate. The apostles, beaten by the council, went out rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame.
“Who accepted no ransom in the path of God.” Hebrews remembers others who were tortured, not accepting deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection.
“Pass beyond fear and hope.” Rábi‘a of Basra prayed for exactly that: to worship neither from fear of hell nor in hope of paradise, but for God’s own sake.
“Enter the Karbila of love manfully, manfully.” Paul’s charge to Corinth has the same ring: stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.

The verse summons the reader to enter a field of death “manfully.” Wilfred Owen, who had watched men die in 1917, calls the sweetness of dying for one’s country the old Lie. What makes the Karbila of love something other than what Owen condemns?
If tranquillity and repose were what is desirable, the holy ones would have chosen them. Milton cannot praise a fugitive and cloistered virtue that never sallies out and sees her adversary.
A cleric cries, “Would that I had been with thee!” at every commemoration. Peter says it to Jesus’s face, though I should die with thee, on the night he denies him three times.

A company weeps for Husayn. Hopkins tells a child grieving over falling leaves what her sorrow is really for: it is Margaret you mourn for. What are mourners of a death thirteen centuries old mourning?
A thousand years of wailing, by those who then did the same to others. Isaiah on worship of that kind: this people draw near me with their mouth, but have removed their heart far from me.
“They rejoice in what they have wrought, even as those who slew Husayn rejoiced.” Jesus tells his disciples beforehand: ye shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice.

The readings condemn those who rejoiced over the slain. Proverbs lays the same rule on the wronged for the day when the tables turn: rejoice not when thine enemy falleth. Is that part of what Karbila teaches?
“It has always been thus - there is nothing new.” The Preacher’s famous line, here turned to comfort: that which hath been is that which shall be.
The reproached are to answer that their martyrs followed those of Karbila. Jesus prepares his followers the same way: if they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you.
“When they speak with vehemence, maintain a oppressed silence.” The First Letter of Peter holds up one who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not.

gibbon-death-of-hosein.text: In a distant age and climate, the tragic scene of the death of Hosein will awaken the sympathy of the coldest reader
gibbon-death-of-hosein.author: Edward Gibbon
gibbon-death-of-hosein.work: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire

homer-priam-kissed-the-hand.text: Fear, O Achilles, the wrath of heaven; think on your own father and have compassion upon me, who am the more pitiable, for I have steeled myself as no man yet has ever steeled himself before me, and have raised to my lips the hand of him who slew my son
homer-priam-kissed-the-hand.author: Homer

micah-o-my-people-what-have-i-done.text: O my people, what have I done unto thee? and wherein have I wearied thee? testify against me

john-for-which-of-those-works.text: Then the Jews took up stones again to stone him. Jesus answered them, Many good works have I shewed you from my Father; for which of those works do ye stone me

matthew-thirsty-and-ye-gave-me-no-drink.text: For I was an hungred, and ye gave me no meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me no drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me not in: naked, and ye clothed me not: sick, and in prison, and ye visited me not

hebrews-not-accepting-deliverance.text: and others were tortured, not accepting deliverance; that they might obtain a better resurrection

psalm-none-to-bury-them.text: O god, the heathen are come into thine inheritance; thy holy temple have they defiled; they have laid Jerusalem on heaps. The dead bodies of thy servants have they given to be meat unto the fowls of the heaven, the flesh of thy saints unto the beasts of the earth. Their blood have they shed like water round about Jerusalem; and there was none to bury them

mark-head-in-a-charger.text: And immediately the king sent an executioner, and commanded his head to be brought: and he went and beheaded him in the prison, And brought his head in a charger, and gave it to the damsel: and the damsel gave it to her mother. And when his disciples heard of it, they came and took up his corpse, and laid it in a tomb

john-the-world-shall-rejoice.text: Verily, verily, I say unto you, That ye shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice: and ye shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy

psalm-vinegar-to-drink.text: Reproach hath broken my heart; and I am full of heaviness: and I looked for some to take pity, but there was none; and for comforters, but I found none. They gave me also gall for my meat; and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink

zechariah-whom-they-have-pierced.text: and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourneth for his only son, and shall be in bitterness for him, as one that is in bitterness for his firstborn

acts-false-witnesses-against-stephen.text: Then they suborned men, which said, We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses, and against God. And they stirred up the people, and the elders, and the scribes, and came upon him, and caught him, and brought him to the council, And set up false witnesses, which said, This man ceaseth not to speak blasphemous words against this holy place, and the law

isaiah-none-to-help.text: And I looked, and there was none to help; and I wondered that there was none to uphold

psalm-joseph-laid-in-iron.text: He sent a man before them, even Joseph, who was sold for a servant: Whose feet they hurt with fetters: he was laid in iron: Until the time that his word came: the word of the Lord tried him

samuel-tell-it-not-in-gath.text: The beauty of Israel is slain upon thy high places: how are the mighty fallen! Tell it not in Gath, publish it not in the streets of Askelon; lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised triumph

quran-help-believers-incumbent.text: Verily We sent before thee (Muhammad) messengers to their own folk. Then we took vengeance upon those who were guilty (in regard to them). To help believers is ever incumbent upon Us.

matthew-what-evil-hath-he-done.text: And the governor said, Why, what evil hath he done? But they cried out the more, saying, Let him be crucified
